Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) a few days ago announced the changes in the subsidy policy concerning fluid milk, he said that it was necessary to give further consideration to the subsidies on milk entering into cheese and into processed milk.

Dairy Products
I am now in a position to state that the subsidy on milk entering into the production of cheese will be increased by ten cents per hundred pounds, that is from 20 cents to 30 cents per hundred pounds, and that the subsidy on milk entering into the production of concentrated milk products and the production of milk sugar will be increased by eight cents per hundred pounds, that is from 15 cents to 23 cents.

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, May 20, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie that the house go into committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Bracken, and the amendment to the amendment of Mrs. Strum.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this debate was adjourned last night I was discussing the amendment and the subamendment, particularly the subamendment which suggests that the workers would not benefit by legislation of this government. I had shown in part what this Liberal government has done in the past for the workers, who may confidently expect similar treatment in the future.
Since the accession of the Liberal party to office in December 1922, labour has been given representation on the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways, Mr. Tom Moore having been appointed a member of the board in that year. The order issued by Mr. D. B. Hanna in 1920 prohibiting employees of the Canadian National Railways from standing as political candidates was withdrawn by Sir Henry Thornton in 1923.
The Civil Service Superannuation Act was passed in 1924. Dominion government policemen and firemen were accorded a weekly rest day in 1924 and 1925 respectively. Persons working for the dominion government on hourly rates were brought within the Public Service Retirement Act in 1922. The Government Employees Workmen's Compensation Act was amended in 1925 to require the payment of the cost of medical aid and hospital expenses to government employees to whom compensation for accident or disease was payable. A further amendment in 1927 provided for dominion government railway employees in Prince Edward Island.
Fishing boats were declared exempt from pilotage dues in 1922. In 1924 children under fourteen were prohibited from being employed, and boys under eighteen forbidden to be employed as trimmers or stokers, on seagoing ships. Provision was made for a compulsory examination of young persons on ships and for unemployment indemnity in case of loss of ships. These amendments to the Canada Shipping Act were based on draft conventions of the international labour conference.
On motion of the Prime Minister in 1924, a standing committee of the House of Commons was appointed to consider the subject of industrial and international relations.
The protection of trade union labels has long been desired by organized labour, since the presence of a union label on articles is considered as a guarantee that the article was manufactured under working conditions governed by an agreement between the employer and the trade union concerned. A bill to give to union labels the same protection as is accorded by the Trade Mark and Design Act to other trade marks was introduced in parliament by the minister of labour and enacted in 1927.
The fair wages policy, adopted in 1900, was made more effective by orders in council passed in 1907, 1922 and 1924. The terms of the labour provisions to be incorporated in government contracts were laid down, making the purpose of the fair wages policy clearer and more definite. Contractors for all government works and supplies are required to pay the rates of wages prevailing in the district in which the work is performed, to post the wages schedule in a conspicuous place, and to keep a record of wage payments available for inspection by the fair wage officers of the Department of Labour. Government departments are required to furnish monthly to the Department of Labour reports giving information as to contracts entered into during the preceding month. This information is published in the Labour Gazette. The fair wages policy of the dominion government for the protection of workers engaged in the execution of federal contracts has been copied in most of the provinces, and by many municipal authorities and other public bodies in Canada. Experience shows that this policy has been of great value to labour in ensuring standard conditions of wages and hours on public works and supplies. In 1929, an order in council required the application of the fair wages order to works in connection with waterpower development in the prairie provinces.
This policy was given statutory effect and extended to provide for an eight-hour day on May 30, 1930, in the Fair Wages and Eight-Hour Day Act. This statute provided that all persons employed by a contractor on government construction works should be paid such wages as are generally accepted as current for competent workmen in the district, provided they are fair and reasonable, and daily hours of work shall not exceed eight except in special cases provided for'by the government or in cases of emergency approved by the minister. Persons employed directly by the government on such work and who are not
Price Ceiling-Farm Products

under the Civil Service Act are to have similar conditions to those laid down for persons employed by contractors. The 1930 act was repealed in 1935 by the Bennett government but was reenacted with the additional restriction of hours to forty-four a week and an extension of its application to works to which the government gives financial assistance.
On March 27, 1930, an order in council stipulated that, except where work is intermittent or the application of the order in council is not practicable, the hours of work of any dominion government employee who at that date was working more than eight hours a day should be reduced to eight with a half holiday on Saturday. In October, 1941, the administration of the fair wages policy was transferred to the national war labour board, but in December, 1943, it was again made the responsibility of the Department of Labour.
The Technical Education Act was enacted-in 1919 under the Conservative regime. Its provisions were based on the recommendations of the royal commission on technical education appointed in 1910 by the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. The act provided for financial assistance to the provinces in promoting technical education for a period of ten years in order to enable them to lay the foundations of a system of technical education.
In 1924, a special committee of the House of Commons was appointed, on the motion of the Prime Minister, to make an inquiry into the need for old age. pensions in Canada. At the legislative session of 1925, after correspondence with the provinces, the committee recommended the adoption of a system of old age pensions, the cost of which should be borne equally by the dominion and the provinces entering into agreements for that purpose.
A piece of legislation which for years was bitterly opposed by labour organizations was section 98 of the criminal code, which was enacted in 1919 following the hysteria of the Winnipeg strike. Its major purpose was to define and deal with "unlawful associations", but labour generally regarded it "as a threat to the civil liberty which Canadians have inherited as their birthright", and also looked upon it as "a curtailment of freedom of speech and assembly". Following representations made by labour bodies, the Liberal government, during the session of 1936, repealed this obnoxious legislation.
In 1937 the Old Age Pensions Act was amended to permit pensions to be., paid to blind persons over forty years of age. The act makes provision for pensions not to exceed $240 a year to British subjects, or widows who
were British subjects before their marriage, who are at least seventy years of age, who have resided in Canada for the twenty years immediately preceding, and in the province concerned for five years preceding, the date on which it is proposed to commence the pension payments, and who are not in receipt of annual income of as much as $365. This legislation has contributed considerably to the lessening of the fear of persons who were blind of becoming destitute, and so helps to assure their future well-being.
The Government Annuities Act enacted in 1908 is administered by the Minister of Labour. An annuity may be purchased by any person resident in Canada. The amount of yearly income may be as low as $10 or as high as $1,200. The cost of the annuity varies with the age of the applicant at the time of purchase and at the time the annuity is to begin, the amount of annuity desired, and whether it is to be payable for a fixed number of years or for life. These government annuities have been purchased by people who are thrifty, hard-working and conscientious. I wonder what the effect would be if we in Canada evolved some inflationary method whereby the value of these annuities, earned with so much hard work, would be reduced-how far these yearly incomes would go.

The Home Improvement Loans Guarantee Act, 1927, permitted the government to guarantee against loss, lending institutions which are approved by the government and which make loans up to a maximum of $2,000 on a single property or $1,000 for each family where more than one family lives on the property, plus $1,000. The government's liability is limited to fifteen per cent of the total amount of loans made by the institution, and may not exceed in all $7,500,000. The Home Improvement Loans Guarantee Act has contributed in my own constituency to the assistance of labour, by providing work and income for a large number of tradesmen.
In 1938 the Shop Cards Registration Act was passed to protect union "shop cards" as union labels were protected by the Trade Mark and Design Act of 1927.
Another enactment of 1938 was the National Housing Act.

In 1939 the criminal -code was amended by the insertion of section 502A, which makes it a criminal offence for an employer to dismiss or refuse to employ a worker for the sole reason he is a member of a trade union or to seek by intimidation or otherwise to prevent an employee from belonging to a trade union. Another enactment of 1939 was the Youth Training Act, which was in effect until March 31, 1943, and under which the dominion government assisted the provinces in carrying out approved schemes for the training of unemployed young persons. The war emergency training programme grew out of the youth training programme.
The Unemployment Insurance Act was passed in 1940, after the British North America Act had been amended to give the dominion parliament jurisdiction in this field. In 1943 the act was amended, the most important change being the removal of the income limit or insurability for persons paid by the piece, hour, day or week, and its extension from $2,000 to $2,400 per year in the case of other employed persons. The possibility of extending the act to various excepted employments is at present under consideration.
In 1942 the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act was passed, replacing an order in council of June, 1941. The Vocational Training Coordination Act was also passed in 1942, to provide for the continuance and development of training already being carried on under the war emergency training and youth training programmes, and also for the training of persons discharged from the armed forces and persons whom the unemployment insurance commission has directed to attend a course of training as provided by the Unemployment Insurance Act.
In 1943, in addition to the amendments I have mentioned in the Unemployment Insurance Act, the National Physical Fitness Act was passed, and an order in council was passed providing a special war supplement for old age and blind pensioners.
In addition to the foregoing, there were statutes for the relief of unemployment, the National Employment Commission Act, 1936, the Youth Training Act, 1939, the National Housing Act, 1938, and the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1940.
An act of 1939 to amend the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act, 1933, provided for compensation to employees deprived of employment or required to take lower-paid employment by reason of cooperative measures by the two railways to effect economy. In 1942 were passed the Vocational Training Coordination Act and the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act.
The first action by the government to provide for as little interruption as possible in war industries as a result of labour disputes was to extend the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, November 7, 1939, to war industries, including industries producing goods essential to the community. A formal declaration of principles for the avoidance of industrial unrest was made by order in council in June, 1940. This "government labour policy" declared the right to freedom of association and urged the making of collective agreements by employers and employed as well as the observance of reasonable wages and hours.
To speed up the settlement of disputes, which were unusually numerous owing to the particular stage which labour organization had reached in Canada, an order in council of June 6. 1941 (P.C. 4020) provided that before a board was appointed under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, an industrial disputes inquiry commission could be appointed to try to settle the difference and, if not successful, to report whether it was desirable to set up a board.
On September 16, 1941, by P.C. 7307, a strike which would hinder the efficient prosecution of the war was made illegal after a board, under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, had reported, until a vote by the employees concerned was taken under the supervision of the Department of Labour and a majority had voted in favour of a strike. Special provision was made to permit the employees of crown companies to join trade unions and to enter into collective agreements with their employers. These orders in council will be suspended, so far as they are inconsistent with the new war-time labour relations regulations, by those regulations.
When the Ontario high court upheld the conviction of a picket under the defence of Canada regulations prohibiting loitering near protected premises, an amendment was made in the regulations to safeguard the right to picket. Labour-management committees, formed to increase production by joint effort, have been encouraged, first by an interdepartmental committee set up a year ago, and now by the industrial production cooperation board, established in January, 1944.
Wages control policy is administered by the national and regional war labour boards, on which employers and labour are represented equally. The cost of living bonus was payable from the time the policy was introduced -October 1941-until the end of 1943, and was designed to protect the basic standard of living. Under the wages control order,

1943, the bonus is to be incorporated in the wage rates but: (a) the Prime Minister has given an undertaking that if the index rises by more than three per cent and remains at that level for more than two consecutive months, the entire stabilization programme will be reconsidered; (b) what was formerly a bonus subject to decrease with a fall in the cost of living is now a ten cent increase in basic rates; (c) the increase in basic rates will be reflected in an increase in overtime rates. As a result of awards of the board,
600,000	workers now receive holidays with pay who did not receive them before the stabilization policy was introduced. Average earnings in the eight leading Canadian industries increased from $26.37 in October, 1941, the month in which the wage control was introduced, to $31.59 in December, 1943-an increase of $5.22 or almost twenty per cent, as compared with an increase of slightly more than three per cent in the cost of living during the same period.
In May, 1941, the minimum rates payable for work on government contracts for the manufacture of supplies were raised from 20 cents per hour for women and 30 cents for men to 25 cents and 35 cents.

speechtext:
In rising to support the amendment of my leader I wish to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, certain matters and conditions which affect the farmer in the part of Ontario in which I reside. The county of Hastings and the county of Peterborough are two very fine agricultural districts. They are ideally suited for mixed farming. Hastings county not only produces more cheese than any other county in the province, but also produces the finest cheese. These factories are located at many points throughout the county, and in addition there are many creameries, a large number of cattle and hogs are produced, as well as a fair number of sheep, poultry and large quantities [DOT] of honey and maple syrup, small fruits and vegetables being also produced and sold.
During the war years the farmers in these two counties made a wonderful contribution to our war effort. The farm supplied a very large number of young men for the armed forces of Canada, and this immediately created *a shortage of farm labour. In these counties, as in all other rural counties, many young men and women left the farm to work in industry, which further complicated the labour situation. Yet, despite this great shortage of labour on 
the farm, the farmers of these counties, in many instances with the assistance of only their wives and children of school age, were able to increase greatly the production of farm products which were so essential during the war years. These farmers carried on without the proper help. In many cases they were unable to replace worn-out machinery. Often it was almost impossible to obtain the necessary farm machinery, repairs. Such aids as tractors, milking machines and other mechanized machinery used on the farm, which would greatly assist where there was a shortage of labour, were not available.
It is true that during the war years there were some slight increases in 'the price of farm products. This was due largely to the payment of- subsidies, just as the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Ilsley) announced1 a few moments ago that there will be a further subsidy on certain classes of milk. Yet while farm products increased slightly, everything that the farmer had to buy in order to operate his farm or live has increased enormously in price. No one can deny to-day that the cost of living has increased from fifty to a hundred per cent, in spite of what the bureau of statistics may say. All one has to do is to ask any mother who had to feed and clothe a family during the war years; none of them will agree that the increase in the cost of living is as shown by the bureau of statistics.
The farmer was obliged to pay greatly increased labour costs. The price of gasoline was higher. The feed which practically every farmer has to buy at some time or other costs him much more, and any material he bought, such as lumber, shingles or hardware, to take care of the necessary repairs or additions, was much higher in price. The cost of skilled labour was at least double. If he had to hire a tractor, a threshing outfit or anything of that nature he had to pay the increased price. A et, as I said before, despite all the hardships and handicaps the farmer and his wife-and in many cases she was his only help -did a splendid job in producing the required food for the men in the armed forces and the civilian population.
We find that to-day conditions have not changed or improved very much. Skilled labour is still scarce, and the wages are still high. It is quite true that it is now easier to purchase farm machinery. Por the first time 'farmers are able to' take delivery of farm machinery; yet the increase of per cent does not help the farmer much. If, as pointed out by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, the farm machineiy companies were entitled to this increase, surely he should

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
have gone a little farther and made out a case to show that the farmer was entitled to an increase in the return for his products.
It appears to me that one of the real causes of the low price of farm products to-day is that when the price ceiling was set in 1941 during the so-called^ basic period, the price of all farm products was very low, which was most unfair to the farmer.
In my county and district the production of cheese in 1945 and 1946 will be away down from previous years. The production of butter is also much less. The hog population has been most seriously reduced. One of the reasons for this is that the farmer is simply reducing his herd of live stock to the point where he can operate the farm alone; for he is no longer able to pay the high wages demanded by farm labourers, if the farm labour were available.
In the matter of income tax we find that in the rural districts the farmer is hounded and worried by the district income tax inspector. During the war in industry a wife who was employed in war work was allowed an extra $660, thereby making a total exemption of $1,860 for a married man. This did not apply to the farmer, whose wife and children were often the only help that he had available. I submit that the time is long past when some change should have been made in the income tax allowances to the end that the individual farmer might be given some extra allowances for the work performed on the farm by his wife and children.
I should like to point out that on the return filed by the farmer there is a heading under the list of receipts which reads:
Miscellaneous sales: . . . cordwood and pulp-wood; posts and lumber; trees, saplings, et cetera; sand, gravel and stone; soil . . .
I cannot understand how anyone, even an income tax official, could take the view that the sale of cordwood, pulpwood, posts, lumber, trees, saplings, sand, gravel, stone and soil can be regarded as income. Surely the sale of these articles from the farm should be regarded as capital. Surely in the lifetime of the average farmer he is not going to get a second crop. If he sells his cordwood and his lumber he is depreciating the value of his farm property or the woodlot by the amount he receives for it. If he sells the soil, the sand, the gravel and the stone, he will never have another crop. I believe that even an income tax official would have to admit that any gravel or sandpit will become exhausted in time.
Another item which appears on the farmers income tax return is: "Produce raised on farm and consumed in the farm home." This item
has always been a contentious one with the farmer, because, as eyeryone will realize, the amount of produce raised and consumed on the farm to-day is much less than it was in years gone by. Yet when they come to deal with the district income tax inspector they find that following his usual autocratic procedure he places this figure at an arbitrary amount for each member of the family, and the farmers pay accordingly. I would point out further that so far as the income tax return of the farmer is concerned he is not allowed any depreciation whatever at the present time for breeding stock.
The small number of returned veterans who are taking advantage of the Veterans Land Act shows that to-day farming has email attraction for them. The number taking up farms is small when compared with the number of veterans who are taking small holdings. While we are on this subject I should like to say to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) that many veterans complain most bitterly about the long delay and the endless red tape in the district offices in regard to applications under the Veterans Land Act. I have some personal knowledge of that, because I have a number of them in my office, and it certainly takes a very long time to get anywhere with them.
In Ontario the provincial hydro electric system is being extended into many new rural areas, so that for the first time the farmer and his wife will have the benefits of cheap hydro electric power. While the farmer has his buildings, including his house, wired for electricity,, he finds that he has to pay the most excessive costs for every type of electrical equipment. Let us, for example, look at the price of an electric stove, which is undoubtedly a necessity, not a luxury. After all, an electric stove is only a few pieces of cheap metal covered with enamel and equipped with elements. Yet when the farmer buys one of those stoves he finds that at the very minimuiti the price is from $250 to $350. The same ratio applies in respect of practically every other type of electrical equipment the farmer has to purchase.
There is one further point I should like to bring out. It seems to me that the activities of the wartime prices and trade board, which operates through its inspectors a type of gestapo throughout the country, checking up on the activities of every small butcher, and producers of every kind, are not doing anything to increase the production of food. In my section of the country we have inspectors from local offices, inspectors from the head office at Brockville, and on very special occasions we are favoured by the
Price Ceiling-Farm Products

presence of inspectors from Ottawa. Not only do they check the stores, but they check the coupons when they go to the banks. Many people have told me recently that they have received letters from the head office at Brock-ville asking for information about the sale of a gallon of syruip, a pail of honey, or perhaps a small quantity of butter. I say in all frankness that the activities of these men, whom I can describe only as gestapo agents, are not relished by the people in the rural districts. They serve only to drive the people into the black market. Certainly they are not such as to encourage the people to cooperate, or to accept willingly these idiotic regulations.
For a number of months in the village of Madoc, in which I reside, we had only one slaughtering permit, owing to the fact that the wartime prices and trade board permit had to be sent to the Belleville office. For a period of more than two months there was no slaughtering permit in that village, with the result that with the exception of some small amounts of pork in the form of bacon and tenderloin received from the packing plants, there was no pork for sale. Despite the fact that the local butcher every second or third day was in touch with the wartime prices and trade board by telephone, or even held interviews with them, nothing could be done.
One unfortunate farmer who sold a pig to the local butcher was dragged down by the gestapo and, with the butcher, landed in court. Only yesterday in that same village the wartime prices and trade board conducted five prosecutions. One of them was against a man who conducts a butcher and grocery business. During the war that man and his wife struggled in every way to hold the business together for their two sons who were serving in the armed forces. But yesterday that man appeared in the police court, charged by the gestapo agents of the wartime prices and trade board because his coupons did not balance. I doubt if anyone conducting a retail business can make his meat, butter, or sugar coupons balance. And it is of special interest that the solicitor who appeared in court yesterday as special prosecutor for the wartime prices and trade board was one of those gutless individuals who obtained exemption from military service in the first great war because of his being a conscientious objector. The sooner the officials who operate the wartime prices and trade board realize they are only antagonizing the public and driving people into the black market, the better it will be for everyone concerned.

It is interesting to note how these officials operate when they descend upon a small village. Generally they move in groups of two or three, depending upon the kind of business they are about to investigate. Then, as in the army, before they descend upon the victim they synchronize their watches and, at a given moment, inspectors walk into each of the butcher shops, or whatever they are investigating, treating the people as they would treat criminals.
These inspectors are running all over the country at the public expense. Unfortunately their activities generally end in the laying of charges. Returns made in this chamber will show the cost of legal fees in connection with the prosecutions, and it is clear that those fees eat up practically the whole of the fines imposed.
It seems unreasonable that the farmer should be asked to continue to bear more than his fair share of the government's stabilization policy. He did so cheerfully during the war, but to-day he simply refuses to continue. After all, the average farmer who spends a lifetime on his farm leaves very little at the time of his death. After practising law for about twenty-five years in the country I have first-hand knowledge as to what the average farmer leaves. In many instances, where farmers and their families have struggled throughout their lives, it is pitiful to see the small amounts in their estates left for their widows.
In conclusion may I say that I intend to support the amendment moved by my leader

Mr. Speaker, such a variety of subjects has been discussed in the debate that one would think there might be nothing left to discuss, and that therefore one must necessarily cover the same ground. However, coming from an agricultural constituency, I find I must say a few words.
There is general dissatisfaction among most of the farmers out west-at least that is the way I find it in my own constituency. They want stabilized prices to compare favourably with the prices of the articles they must buy. The greatest trouble to-day is that the prices of the commodities the farmers have to sell are almost stationary, while those of commodities they must buy are advancing almost every day. We had a good illustration of that recently in the increase of 12J per cent in the price of farm machinery, coming at a time when most of the farmers are in the market for new machinery. During the war they were unable to buy the machinery they required, and had the old ones patched up.

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
Quantities of hay-wire the farmers had accumulated in the bad years were used for that purpose.
Along with the increased machinery prices went an increase in the price of gasoline. I think I am right when I say that the price of everything the farmers have to buy is going up, including machinery, fuel oil, and lumber. Besides, the lumber is of inferior quality; it is wet and hardly fit for use. The farmer must pay increased prices for his clothing and most of the groceries he has to buy. Naturally in view of these conditions there are many complaints.
We have heard a good deal about the production of grains and live stock going down. This is true of my area. In 1942 we had an average yield of fourteen bushels to the acre, which is a good average for the drought areas of southern Alberta. If they had that yield in the northern part of the province they would consider it more or less of a failure, but we are not used to high yields in the south. The fall of 1942 was quite wet and a considerable amount of grain spoiled. It was combined when it was damp; the farmers, not being able to dispose of the grain under the wheat quota system, had to put it in bins, and some of it was partly heated. Of course that could be used only to feed live stock, and therefore the farmers went into the production of hogs. Many farmers in my area who had never had a "hog on their farms went quite heavily into hog raising, many of them having as many as two hundred hogs. As soon as the 1942 crop had been fed or disposed of, they entered again into the dry years. 1943 and 1944 were poor years, but 1945 was poorer still, and the farmers found themselves with no feed. I think this accounts largely for the reduction in the production of hogs in my area. We know that in other areas where feed was available the farmers have gone out of the production of hogs because of the increased prices brought about by the subsidies on barley and oats, there being very little wheat fed to hogs. The 1945 production of grains and all live stock, both hogs and cattle, was down. I should like to read a newspaper clipping under date of November 1, 1945, in which the Minister of Agriculture is reported as follows:
Agriculture minister Gardiner announced yesterday that under provisions of the Prairie Barm Assistance Act the 1945 crop year has been declared an emergency year and assistance will be given farmers whose crops have suffered from drouth and other causes.
He said more than 3,000 townships in the eastern half of Alberta and the western half of Saskatchewan had suffered from the severest drouth since 1937. Without' aid under the
P.F.A. "thousands of farmers otherwise would be unable to carry on" until the next crop was harvested.
Since the act was passed in 1939 the only crop year which has not been declared an emergency year was that of 1942-43.
Assistance payments under this act derived from a fund to which each farmer contributes one per cent of' the amount he receives on grain sales each year. These contributions to date have constituted more than one-third of the assistance payments made since the act came into force and the remainder was provided by funds from the treasury of Canada.
This shows that production was down over a very wide area. In those 3,000 or more townships the average yield of wheat was less than four bushels per acre. When the yield is below four bushels there is not much to cut, but the farmers go out with their combines to save what they can. Many farmers got only enough for seed.
What I have said makes it clear that we should press for irrigation in this area. In comparison with the low production in these areas during the last three years I would refer hon. members to what happened on a tract of land 250 acres in extent along the South Saskatchewan river which has been under the control of the dominion government for about three years. A press report reads:
The dominion government will profit this year by about $39,000 through the Golden Valley farm, a 250-acre tract near Medicine Hat, operated by the Medicine Hat internment camp. German prisoners of war interned at the camp provide all the labour for the farm. Products from the vegetable farm-the largest in Alberta -go to military establishments in the province through the district supply office of military district No. 13.
This shows what can be done when water is pumped on the land or there is an irrigation system. That farm was operated with the help of German prisoners of war, and it is really worth seeing. The same applies to the Lethbridge area, where sugar beets and other crops are raised. I often think that the farmers around Medicine Hat have more courage than anyone else, because they will continue to put in a crop year after year and pray for rain which never comes. It is a "next year" country. Every spring they go out and put in a crop which usually comes up nice and green. But quite often, as occurred this spring, we have dust storms almost every other day and thousands of acres of grain'are ruined. But the farmers always hope that they will have a crop, until along about the first part of July the hot chinook winds come along and the temperature will run to about one hundred in the shade for a number of weeks without cooling off at nights. Then the farmers must sit back and watch their crops wither and dry up.

When you get into the irrigated areas it is entirely different. Last year in the Taber-Lethbridge area they harvested 362,000 tons of sugar beets from which the farmers received a good income. I should like to read another press report published in Lethbridge on April 10, 1946, as follows:
A second subsequent sugar beet payment, amounting to nearly $100,000 now is in the mails for more than 1,300 farmers who raised sugar beets in southern Alberta last year. The payment represents 25 cents a ton on the 1945 production of 362,000 tons, and brings returns to growers on their 1945 beets to $8.80 so far. The growers received an initial payment of $8 and a first subsequent payment of 55 cents a ton late last year.
The farmers in that area are prosperous. When they sow a crop they have something to harvest.
The cattle producers in my area are more or less dissatisfied. There is a price ceiling, of course, in the butcher shops, but the farmer
who takes in his stock may receive 12 dollars one day and 11 dollars the next day. These fluctuations are bad for the farmers. I want to read a letter that I received from a large rancher in my district. He runs about 1,500 head of cattle. He grows very little grain- only enough for feed. This is what he says in his letter:	.
It is hard to convince those fellows down there that there is anything important west of the great lakes.
There is no doubt we are headed for real trouble in the cattle business. I can never understand the big fluctuations in the price of live cattle when there is a definite ceiling and floor on the beef. The consumer never gets it any cheaper, whatever the price of live cattle might be.
Another very interesting sidelight on the markets this year, at least to me. was the prices paid for ranch cattle. Most of the ranch steers I know of sold from 11-50 to 12 dollars weighed at the ranch. This means 50 to 75 cents a hundred more than on the market as it costs about that to put them on the market. My own steers sold for 11-75 at home. At that time choice steers in Winnipeg were quoted at 11 dollars. While I was very pleased to get $1.50 over the market I couldn't see any reason for it, unless the packers wanted to keep us quiet as we are the only organized producers that seem to object very strongly to the way the market is handled.
He belongs to the Western Stockgrowers association and to the Short Grass association, so in that way they are organized. The ranchers, of course, received a better price for - their cattle. That may be due to the fact that they raise larger numbers, and on the average they may have a better class of cattle. The writer of this letter has 1,500 head of well-bred Hereford cattle; every one of them is whitefaced. We have other large ranchers in that country, one running 3,500 head of cattle and another about 4,000, These cattlemen will tell
you that they have made money during the war, but they suffered plenty in the bad years before the war from low prices.
It was amusing to me the other night to hear the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Sinnott) discussing the prices paid under different governments. He quoted the prices paid in 1929 when the Liberal government was in power and the prices paid in the nineteen thirties when the Conservative government was in power, but he failed to mention what the present government paid for cattle in the fall of 1937 in their dominion cattle-buying scheme. One cent a pound is what was paid for cattle at that time, when the present government was in power. The price of hogs was down too; everything was down. I was out on that scheme along with dominion buyers, and I know what it was. I spent about a month with them going from one town to another organizing the buying days and taking applications from farmers to sell cattle. So, after all, the present government's record in the matter of prices is not good. I know it is the habit for a member to praise or condemn the government according to which side he supports, and he does not present the whole case.
I also heard the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. McCuaig) mention the price of wheat in the spring of 1938. He was speaking of the price of seed wheat supplied by the wheat board to the farmers in the drought area. I had a large part in that work as provincial inspector in the area from which I come. I issued 52,000 bushels of seed wheat on relief at 11.48 a bushel to farmers in that area. That fall, when the farmers went to sell their wheat, it wa$ down to 50 cents a bushel. That is why farmers want stabilized prices. They have had all they want of a speculative market. The farmers have paid back these seed grain accounts, and that says a lot for the farmers. I had the pleasure of collecting most of that money, and the farmers had the pleasure of being able to pay it back. It is true that many objections were made to having to pay back at the rate of three bushels for every one bushel they received, but that is the nature of the farmers in that drought area.
We hear a lot of complaints from farmers about the income tax. While it is true that a large number of farmers in that area have not a large enough income to pay income tax, there are many others who do pay income tax, and they feel that the exemptions are not high enough, and rightly so; I agree with them on that. We should do what we can to. raise the income tax exemptions not only for the farmers but for the workers as well. The man

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
who has been really hard hit by the income tax is the man on straight salary, as I was myself when I was working for the provincial government. We had no opportunity of chiselling, if I might use the word. We received our cheques every month with ninety per cent of the tax deducted, and if the tax had not been deducted at the source I am sure it would have been impossible for many of us to pay the income tax at the end of the year. The farmers are in exactly the same plight. They want the income tax exemptions raised, and they should be raised.
Prairie farm assistance has been a big help to many of those farmers. It has been their main means of livelihood in the last three years. If it had not been for that, many of them would have been forced on relief. So when they come out and fight for stabilized prices I feel they are fighting for something they should have. Stabilized prices must bear some relation to what the farmer has to pay for the things he buys.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words concerning the question now under debate. In recompense for the period of sacrifice through which they lived during the war, the farmers are entitled to enjoy all possible protection and assistance from the government. Prices of agricultural products must be maintained at a reasonable level, and the cost of farm implements must not be increased in the most difficult times which are experienced by the farming community and, indeed, by every class of the Canadian people. If you increase the price of farm implements you necessarily raise the cost of production, and the fullest agricultural production is essential to the salvation of the world at this decisive moment. By every possible means, and particularly by expanding production and extending markets, the government must help the farmer. I wish to point out that it is quite impossible for the average farmer to make out income tax reports, and at the last session I asked the government to appoint accountants to help him. This would be in the public interest, as well as in the interest of the government.
(Translation): Mr. Chairman, I know my people's needs and am against the maintenance, in peace-time, of a dictatorship established during the war. The duly elected representatives of the people have been supplanted, in Canada, by a bureaucracy. Such a dictatorship paralyses activities in every sphere of our national life.
We are resorting to the very totalitarian methods which Canada has fought to the
limit of her resources. A parliament elected to serve rather than enslave the people has had to yield its supremacy to commissions enjoying unrestricted power, although not responsible to the people. State paternalism is being established permanently and forever within the intricate machinery of government. Canada, with its planned economy, is progressing towards socialism. Our government is continually resorting to controls. Free enterprise and trade are being jeopardized by the anti-social attitude of a powerful clique of bureaucrats, while our civilian population greatly lacks life's very essentials. Farmers cannot secure agricultural implements without which they are unable to cultivate their land. The government has just abolished the consumers' milk subsidy, and yet milk is surely not considered a luxury. It is indispensable to every child's growth and health. The very shortage of food and other goods would seem to justify controls. And yet controls are the best means of increasing the scarcity of foodstuffs and industrial products. Due to a controlled and misdirected economy almost four hundred thousand persons are now unemployed in Canada. And in this upheaval of this country's social and economic security, the government seems to ignore the prerogatives and the jurisdiction of the provinces.
I alluded a moment ago to the increase in the prices of farm machinery. It would be interesting to recall .the words uttered in this House on May 2, 1938, by the Hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), which are found on page 2429 of Hansard:
Agriculture, which is the greatest primary industry in Canada, refuses to be bled any longer by half a dozen manufacturing plants which give as their only real reason the fact that they are employing 4,159 men.

Mr. Speaker, I listened attentively to what the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Probe) had to say. I was pleased to hear his first statement, that the question before the house to-day is a very broad one indeed and takes in a lot more than just the motion before the house and the amendment. He stated specifically that anybody who voted against the motion or against the amendment voted against the principle of controls as they are applied to-day. So that the motion before the house is distinctly a motion of nonconfidence in the present administration. It is in that aspect that I view the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken).
As I said, this question is a very broad one. It did not start last week. It is a storm that has been growing over a long time. There has been constant pressure on the government to remove the controls. There came to my mind, when considering this question, a speech that I had read some time ago by Mr. Burton, president of the Robert Simpson Company Limited, who I think was the first responsible man to start the ball rolling. In a famous speech which attracted a great deal of attention in this country he specifically and clearly stated:
Row that the war is over, controls over wages and prices are no longer needed nor are they in the public interest.
The ball started from there more or less. Later on, many of the larger companies in this country followed suit. I have here a circular letter of the Searle Grain Company Limited on price regulation in which it is clearly stated:
When commodities become scarce, prices rise, and so curtail consumption and tend to induce greater production, which is what is needed to restore the balance or equilibrium. When commodities become too plentiful or in excess of demand, then prices fall and so tend to induce greater consumption, which in turn automatically tends to clear away surpluses, and to reduce production, all of which helps to restore a better balance between supply and demand. Freely moving prices, therefore, as registered on open commodity markets, tend to regulate the economic activities of man in quite a successful way on the average, and in a manner that tends to ensure the proper quantity of production of any commodity needed by the people, and that amount of consumption required to clear away surpluses. No governmental method of planning, or of "fixed" price, has ever been able for long to accomplish these important functions.

I have given these quotations to show the pressure that has been put on the government lately to remove controls. Later on, the Progressive Conservative party in convention ratified that principle. Shortly afterwards the leader of the opposition made a speech in which he announced that he was fully behind the removal of price control and now finally we have this motion of non-confidence in the government, which is the first shot fired to blow away the ceiling in this country. The position, therefore, of the government and of the official opposition in this house is quite clear, and cannot be mistaken. I know that hon. gentlemen opposite are sincere in their belief. They do not believe in controls.
I must admit that the removal of controls frightens me dreadfully, because I still have in mind the dreadful consequences of the period of inflation that followed the first great war. If we were to remove the ceilings on all farm products it would not be long before we would have no controls at all in Canada. I think everybody realizes that if we were to remove controls on the primary products of agriculture, the major industry of this country, all ceilings and all controls would go sooner or later. So that if the decision has to be made, it must be made now. Coming from Manitoba as I do, I am quite satisfied that if the controls were removed to-day the small progress which our farmers have been able to make in the last decade would certainly be lost, and they would slide back to where they were in the inflationary period after the last war. Surely we have not forgotten the experience of the past. I have here an editorial from the Winnipeg Free Press, by Grant Dexter, dated April 19, 1941, which reviews the picture so far as prices after the first great war are concerned. I quote:
Cash wheat prices on May 11 and 12, 1917 (No. 1 northern) stood at $3 a bushel. Control came Sept. 12, and $2.12 was paid for the 1917 crop, $2,294 on 1918 crop, and $2.63 on 1919 crop. After control was lifted, cash wheat went to $2.85 before the crash in prices began. Barley-reached $1.68; oats, 93 cents, flax seed, $4.80 (It had been $6), hay, $40 per ton, cattle, 16 cents on the hoof, hogs, $23.74 per hundredweight. Butter was selling at 75 cents per pound; eggs topped $1.25 per dozen; sugar, 30 cents per pound; potatoes, $2.60 per bag; fresh ham, 46 cents per pound; fresh bacon, 474 cents; cured ham, 504 cents; cured bacon, 584 cents.
Returned soldiers found that the bonus paid on their discharge from the army did little more than buy them a civilian outfit.
Food prices might seem good for the farmers. But on the contrary, the farmers declared that the prices they were receiving -were ruinously low. Middlemen, they said, were reaping fortunes. Their costs of production had risen enormously.
The wave of industrial unrest reached heights never equalled before or since .... The One Big Union movement flared up rapidly. The

Winnipeg strike made many people think the country was ripe for revolution. The inflation ran its course to the inevitable and equally disastrous collapse.
This is the story as it stood after the last war; and surely we cannot close our eyes to the realities of the present time. There is nothing that can lead us to believe that the situation is any different this time. The worst of the inflation after the last war did- not come, nor did the necessity for control come actually during the period of the war, but in the period immediately following the war. So I maintain that it is definitely the responsibility of this government to face the storm and put up a fight to maintain stability in this country.
As far as I am concerned, there is no question of doubt as to where I stand on this issue, and I think I am right in assuming that it is pretty well the position of all western members, at least on this side of the house. This attitude of the west is quite clearly defined, at least in my province, in the newspapers. I think I may quote again from the Winnipeg Free Press, because there is an editorial here which puts the picture of controls quite well. I quote from the issue of that newspaper of May 17 an editorial entitled, "The need for controls":
If there is one thing very clear, it is that the government is moving as well as it can toward the abolition of controls. It is also clear that certainly the particular set of bureaucrats involved in this problem are all very eager to wind up their jobs. Meanwhile, however, they have to hang on. . .
Too great haste in taking off the controls would inevitably result in the defeat of the major objective sought by the price and wage policy of the government. We have emerged from the war stronger and more stable^ in our economic structure than any other major belligerent. We have kept so well on balance that, if we can but exercise continued skill and patience, we will be able to escape many of the ills and dangers that beset us on all sides.
The wartime prices and trade board is effecting what might be called a fighting retreat, holding each line up to the point where the rising flood of supplies makes further control unnecessary. In attempting this difficult manoeuvre it is obvious that mistakes will be made and that injustices will arise. This is inevitable.
But the over-all gain to Canada of maintaining the controls is far greater than any of the vexatious mishaps which take place from time to time. The pressure to remove the controls is very great. It comes, to too great an extent, from pofiticiains who seek an easy platform success, by wanton utterance. They appeal to the narrow interests of the group they happen to be addressing and thereby neglect the national interest. In war time, greatly to the nation's credit, such appeals were ignored. They are far more dangerous to-day when the inspiration and- discipline of war have vanished or grown stale. A further effort is needed.

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
Some might say that this is the opinion of a newspaper which, is on the whole, considered favourable to the government. But I have here another clipping, from the editorial page of the Winnipeg Tribune, and the stand of that newspaper on this issue is also quite clear. I quote from the Tribune of May 7, 1946:
Perhaps Canadian efforts toward holding down living costs are best appreciated when compared with those made in the United States. Price control was introduced in that country later than in the dominion. Moreover, the office of price administration, the United States equivalent of the wartime prices and trade board, has not met with the same measure of government or public support accorded the wartime prices and trade board in Canada. In fact,
O.P.A's very existence was threatened recently in congress.
The following table compiled by the Windsor Star and quoted in an editorial by the Edmonton Journal is indicative. Windsor and Detroit, just across the river from each other, offer an excellent opportunity for comparison of the two countries' successes or failures in battling rising living costs. Here is the table of comparisons of current costs of every-day items in the two centres:
Soft drinks: Windsor, 7 cents; Detroit, 10-15 cents.
Hamburgers, hot dogs: Windsor, 10 cents; Detroit, 21 cents.
Telephone, two-party full service: Windsor, $2.85 per month; Detroit, $5-$6 per month.
Electricity, average for family of four: Windsor, $5-$6 for two months; Detroit, $16-$24 for two months.
Haircuts: Windsor, 50 cents; Detroit, 75 cents to $1.
Shave:	Windsor, 25 cents; Detroit, 50-60
cents.
Downtown movie:	Windsor, 45-85 cents;
Detroit, 85 cents.
Two persons on evening out (one drink each, dinner, movie, coffee, doughnuts, bus fare): Windsor, $3.47; Detroit, $9.10.
Butter:	Windsor, 42 cents to 44 cents; Detroit, 56 cents to 60 cents.
And so on.
The difference in prices in the two cities should not lead to complacency on the part of Canadians. Greater pressures than ever before are threatening to break our price ceilings. Indeed, the greatest threat lies in the fact that the Canadian economy is bound up with that of the United States. It will be only with the greatest difficulty that our price structure is kept from going hog wild if American prices advance much more.
Price control is still a full-time job for Canadians.
To complete the record I will read from the Winnipeg News, which reflects, I believe, the labour side of the story, because this release is entitled "Winnipeg News on labour view of prices board policy." It reports resolutions adopted by 1,600 labour liaison representatives, representing approximately 600,000 trade unionists across Canada. Here is the report:
General approval of wartime prices and trade board policies and suggestions that the board should only remove controls from articles in
good supply and that the present standards division of the board be continued as a permanent part of government organization was voiced in a five-point resolution passed by over thirty labour liaison officers to the board's consumer branch, at a conference held Wednesday night in the board offices.
Included in the five-point resolution are these statements:
1.	The wartime prices and trade board has done a creditable job in controlling prices, rationing and other phases of its work.
2.	The W.P.T.B. has been the medium which has saved citizens of Canada, particularly labour men and women, millions of dollars by preventing inflation.
I will not take the time of the house to read the other items of the resolution, but I may say that they are along the same line, and prove that these liaison officers of the labour movement certainly recognize the great benefits of the wartime prices and trade board to this country, and more specifically, I would say, in its application to western Canada, because I hold that we are much more vulnerable from this point of view.
I do not think there is any question as to the stand of the western people at the present time. Everyone remembers quite well the heavy burden left on the shoulders of the people of the prairies by the inflation that took place after the last war, and such inflation is probably more damaging in connection with farm land in the prairies. I am thinking now of ail the young people and middle-aged persons as well who left the prairies during the war to go and work in the factories in the east as well as on the coast. Statistics prove that there was an exodus from the prairie provinces during the war, and it is my contention that those people will come back to the prairies. Surely, therefore, if any more inflation js allowed at the present time, they will not have a ghost of a chance of settling in the prairies, and even if they did try to buy land at any higher prices than those charged at the present time they would have no chance of succeeding. Therefore, in the interests of the economy of the west, it is absolutely essential, I would say, that controls remain clamped on.
Another factor to be considered is the Veterans Land Act. No doubt a large number of young veterans will settle on land in the prairies. Statistics reveal that so far there have not been very many, but we must remember that the war ended not long ago, and as a matter of fact I know that the applications have been far too many for what the department has been able to cope with. I am quite satisfied that there are a good many veterans who are getting an education which they could not afford in the thirties, and as
Price Ceiling-Farm Products

soon as their knowledge has improved and they have obtained education they will try to settle on the land in greater numbers. We should not do anything to make it impossible for them to settle on the land; we should at least leave the opportunity open.
When we mention the land settlement act,
I perforce am compelled to think of the success or otherwise of the soldier settlement board-because it is wise to look back. Of course the two cannot be compared, since one is a great improvement on the other; but though that act may not have been all that it should have been, the main reason why the Soldier Settlement Act did fail-and certainly -it failed in my constituency and province- was that prices were inflated when those veterans tried to settle on the land. The picture of this enterprise is certainly far from being a bright one. In fact, it is very gloomy, more particularly, for one reason, or another, in Manitoba.	.
Even to-day, however, in spite of the fact that prosperity in the west is quite relative, there is a marked tendency for land to go up in price. I am not going to quote figures, although I have them for the various provinces, comparing 1939 with 1944 and 1945. They are most conservative, and they show an increase in Canada, from 1939 to 1945, of 20 per cent. In its interpretation of the figures, however, the bureau of statistics say that they are very conservative and that it seems likely that these estimates understate the gains that-have actually occurred in Canada.
I remember an article which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press and in the Tribune putting the rise in the cost of land up to 50 per cent. So that if we take the middle course between the two, there is no question that there has been an increase in price in farm land in the west; and that if controls were removed, land would undoubtedly soar in price, and this would not be to the advantage of the people living in the west or of those who wish to become reestablished in the prairies.
At this stage I wish to commend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and I also wish to give all the encouragement I can to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) to hold the line down, whatever the cost. I commend the Minister of Agriculture for embarking a few years ago on the policy of giving, not exceedingly high prices but stabilized prices, even to the point of sacrificing high prices for stability. The farmers and all other people in the west are one class, because everyone depends upon the main industry of agriculture, and everyone to-day sees the wisdom of having stabilized agriculture in the prairies. I am sure we got that impression in this house when
(Mr. Jutras.J
bill No. 5 was being discussed. It was apparent from those who spoke on that bill-those members from the west-that they did not want to be left to the speculation of a few but wanted the income of the farmer put on a stablized basis even to the point of being controlled, whether in connection with the wheat board or the wartime prices and trade board.
There is an absolute necessity to enforce these controls if we wish to have a stabilized economy in the west. It is the only way, because we have tried other means. Apparently it is the only way by which we can be relatively prosperous in the country.
When I speak of controls, I do not mean that we must maintain controls indefinitely, because that has not been the policy of the government, and as time goes on they can be relaxed when possible. Of course I am not in a position to judge exactly the time or the item. That is the responsibility of the Minister of Finance. He is a capable man and he has shown that he can do a good job. I am satisfied to leave the responsibility to him, be' cause I know he will look after the interests of the Canadian people, and that includes my people.
After all, in this world we have to put our confidence in somebody or something and I am content to put my confidence in the efforts of the Minister of Finance. The Prime Minister, in explaining the policy of the government on price and wage control, on January 31, 1946, made the position of the government quite clear. I quote two short passages so that the government's attitude may appear on the record.
In moving toward the period when price control is no longer necessary, the government believes that subsidy payments should continue to be kept to a minimum and eliminated as promptly as is feasible. Thei'e is a great deal of difference between a gradual and planned policy of adjustment to post-war conditions, which may involve some modest increase in prices, and a policy of rapid removal of anti-inflation controls. The objective of the government's policy is to continue to protect the people of Canada from a sharp upswing in prices and living costs, and from the inevitable aftermath of deflation, unemployment and distress. Its purpose is to protect the value of wages and war-time savings. It is aimed to help to open larger markets both at home and abroad, and thus hasten progress toward the high level of peacetime production and employment which is our leading economic objective. With the intelligent support of the Canadian people Canada's anti-inflation programme will achieve its aim. It will bring our country through the most destructive war in history and its aftermath without the economic and social disruption which have been the sorry heritage of past conflicts.
The duty of the government is quite clear. If one looks back at what the government has done so far he will see that it is just a

Private Bills
bare and simple implementing of what it said it would do. I realize that controls in themselves are not popular. Somebody has to take the responsibility of maintaining them. I repeat, it is the responsibility of the government, and I hope that they will have the courage to stand by it.
I should like to give a brief picture of the position of agriculture in the three western provinces, and try to indicate how they appear under a controlled economy such as we have had in the last-few years. I hold in my hand a report issued by the dominion mortgage and investment association. This association is made up of thirty of the large mortgage and investment companies in Canada. It comprises most of the sum total of the mortgages which are held by the farmers of the three western provinces. I shall quote the first part which gives a picture of the conditions existing in the last year. This is the report for 1946 and reads as follows:
Farmers in tile three prairie provinces reduced their mortgage and agreement for sale debts by 26 per cent in 1945. This estimate is based on the experience of thirty life insurance, trust and loan companies which have a substantial investment in farm mortgages and agreements for sale in the prairie provinces. The farms which are security for these mortgages are located in all sections of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. Thus the experience of these companies can be taken as representative of that of all farm mortgage investors in western Canada.
As was to be expected, .payments of mortgage principal and interest by farmers in the prairie provinces were lower in 1945 than in 1944. This would have been the case even if farm cash income had not declined since the total amount owing at the beginning of 1945 was substantially less than at the beginning of 1944.
In view of the reduction which occurred in farm cash income, payments of principal and interest were maintained at a high level. Farm cash income for the three prairie provinces dropped from $1,033 million in 1944 to $847 million in 1945, a reduction of $186 million, or 18 per cent. Principal and interest payments as a percentage of the total amount owing were greater in 1945 than in any previous year with the exception of 1944.
The total amount owing to the thirty companies by farmers in the three prairie provinces on farm mortgages and agreements for sale declined 26-1 per cent in 1945. The reduction in the amount owing by Manitoba farmers was 25'4 per cent; by Saskatchewan farmers, 25-6 per cent; and by Alberta farmers, 28 per cent. The reduction in the amount owing since the end of 1937 is remarkable. It is doubtful if any other group in Canada has been as successful in reducing their liabilities during the past eight years as have the farmers of the prairie provinces. The total amount owing on mortgages and agreements for sale by farmers in the prairie provinces is now considerably less than half what it was at the end of 1937-the percentage reduction being 60 per cent. In Manitoba, the decrease since the end of 1937 is 67 per cent; in Saskatchewan, 57 per cent, and in Alberta 65 per cent.
These large decreases have been achieved bv thousands of farmers reducing substantially the amount they owe by way of farm mortgages and agreements for sale and by thousands of others paying off their mortgages entirely. During the past eight years the number of farmers in the prairie provinces who own their farms entirely free of debt has increased very materially.
At the end of 1945 there were 6,339 fewer farmers in debt to these thirty companies by way of mortgages and agreements for sale than at the end of 1944. As compared with the end of 1937, the reduction in the number of farmers in debt to these thirty companies is 27,671, or more than fifty per cent.
The annual report of this association for 1943 made reference to the estimate of total farm debt in the three prairie provinces made by Professor W. J. Waines of the university of Manitoba for the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations. He estimated total farm debt in Manitoba at $108-7 million, $432-5 million in Saskatchewan, and $265-1 million in Alberta, a total of $806-3 million. Since it is a well established fact that farmers use increased income to liciuidate current indebtedness before applying it to long-term indebtedness such as mortgage debt, it is a reasonable assumption that total farm debt in the prairie provinces has declined just as fast as mortgage debt. It would appear, therefore, that total farm debt in the prairie provinces has declined by more than $450 million in the past eight years.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before six
o'clock I had just dealt with the report of the various loan companies in the west, showing what had been accomplished in western Canada over the last seven years, I want to say immediately that hon. members should not jump to conclusions. While it is true that I did mention that the picture was much brighter in the west than it was before, I merely pointed out that farmers had paid 50 per cent of their indebtedness over the last seven years. That implies that they are still 50 per cent in debt. They are in the process of digging themselves out of the hole at the present time. But we must remember that agriculture has gone through a period of debt and disaster. I.hasten to point out that this achievement of the last seven years has not been accomplished by taking trips to California, or by playing bridge, or even by reading Hansard during the winter months on the prairies, as was suggested by some hon. members. It has been accomplished through toil and sweat, by their own hands, while their sons and daughters were fighting the war overseas.
It does not mean, either, that they are making large profits at the present time. As a matter of fact they are making very small profits. But it is mostly the fact that there is a small profit in all the various aspects of agriculture which accounts for the picture I have drawn. To my mind it is a' case of a little here and a little there.
In my view it is time the Canadian people revised their thinking so far as agriculture is concerned. There are too many city people who think of prices of agricultural products in terms of prices during the depression. At the present time, because it has been said that the price of milk will be twelve cents in the city, a wave of protest has arisen in some cities. I suggest that the people of Canada are getting the very best of food, and. so far as milk is concerned they are getting a much

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
improved product. I do not consider twelve cents a quart is too much or too high a price to pay for such a good product. Too many - people forget that to-day milk has to be pasteurized and homogenized. It must be delivered in sterilized containers; it must come from T.B-tested cows. It must be subjected to quick cooling after milking, because of the factor of acidity. Then there is a deduction made from the price if it does not reach 3'5 per cent butterfat. It must be delivered to the door-and delivered before breakfast, in the wee, small hours of the morning. So that when one compares milk with soft drinks, with tea and coffee or with fruit juices, or with any of the various food products, including luxury beverages, I do not think the price of milk is too high.
While I am not offering this as a case in point, I must maintain that too many people in the cities are thinking in terms of prices they paid in the years of depression. At that time farmers were generous enough to give away their product because they could not keep it and could not sell it. So they just made a gift of it to the people. Those conditions are, we hope, gone. Had I the time I would deal with this matter more fully. However, I trust I shall have another opportunity to do so.
At the present time I wish to deal briefly with the C.C.F. amendment. I know that in that party there are a few competent farmer members who are sincere in their convictions. However, it would appear from the amendment presented to the house that in that group they are but a small minority. I wish to give full credit to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mrs. Strum), who moved the amendment to the amendment, for her sincerity in doing so. I admit the sincerity of the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), who seconded the motion, but I would point out that the diversion of opinion between the two differs just as greatly as the diversion of opinion between any of the parties in this house. No doubt the hon. member for Cape Breton South appealed to the motherly instincts of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle in order to have her add the word "workers" and gather under the protection of her wing all the people of Canada. But be it as it may, it would appear that the hon. member for Qu'Appelle in wording her amendment in that way serves one purpose only, that is, to confuse the issue. I ask: What burden does an increase in prices of farm implements impose upon the workers of Canada? It is just a case of, "he is getting it, we want it too." It is simply a demonstration that within the ranks of the C.C.F., labour is the dominating factor.

Just before the six o'clock recess the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Probe) was pointing out that the C.C.F. party were unanimous about the question of controls. I should like to refer briefly to what the seconder had to say about the great concern he had over controls.
In connection with the cost of living he said, as reported at page 1557 of Hansard'.
There is also a difference in the cost of living; I realize that, but it is not equal to the differential in the income of the workers. I do not care how high the cost of living goes.
Here is what he had to say about inflation, a matter about which I feel very deeply:
There is a whole lot of the bogey man in this business of inflation. I am not very much afraid of it.

This business of waving that flag of inflation is overdone. A little inflation is good, if it does not get away from you. Then to show his concern over the increase in farm prices, he said this:
Do not forget that about eighty or eighty-five per cent of the cash handled by the average small-salaried man or wage-earner in this country is spent on food, clothing and shelter, particularly on food. The point I was going to make is this. As I said a moment ago, President Truman ordered an upward trend in wages in order that the people might have purchasing power, because if they cannot buy we are going to have unemployment. The trend in Canada is the reverse.

That shows the confidence the hon. member has in price controls. Then he goes on to say:
The farmer asks for increased prices. Fine; I agree with that. I believe those prices have to be stepped up. But when we increase the price of farm products we automatically increase the cost of living.
The hon. member had said just previously that he did not mind the cost of living going up, and he then goes on to refer to the industrial worker:
And that comes back to the industrial worker. If farm prices are going up, then in proportion to those increases in farm prices we have to increase the wage structure if we are to keep on an even keel. Unless this is done, the effect will be that of dumping an additional load on the shoulders of the small salaried worker.
I am sure that is not what the hon. member for Qu'Appelle had in mind in her amendment. Let me say in conclusion that if that represents the unanimous opinion of the C.C.F. towards agriculture, it is a pretty poor show indeed.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened carefully to the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras) and I want to compliment him upon the excellent speech he has made. I noticed that he was careful not to get too close to the issue and further confuse the house. I observed that he mentioned chiefly the doughnuts that were served in Windsor and the cocktails that were served in Detroit, as well as many of the things that are not even produced in Provencher. Generally speaking, his remarks were in keeping with the policy of the government of the day.
This issue concerns more lives in the Dominion of Canada and throughout the world than perhaps any other issue that has been presented to this house this session. Everyone within sound of my voice as well as everyone in Canada knows that there is nothing more vital to maintaining the peace that we have achieved at such a great cost. When we realize the malnutrition that exists among the children of Europe to-day, when we realize the lack of housing for the boys who fought the battles overseas; when we realize the demand for consumer goods and the failure in production, then we know that we are face to face with a crisis in the affairs of this dominion, a crisis more concerned with production than any other crisis in our history.
I make no apology for speaking on this issue. You, Mr. Speaker, have been in this house almost as long as I, although you are many years younger. I think you will have observed how consistently I have supported a policy of greater production. I think you will recall as will the erstwhile leader of the party

. opposite, that some years ago I urged the government to stop its policy of non-production and get ready for the days of peace. You will recall, and I certainly recall having said that food would win the war and food would save the peace. That cry, which was uttered by many others on this side, fell on deaf ears.
I speak as a member of the party that is recognized in Canada to-day as being the farmers' party. We have not a farmer as our leader simply because he is a farmer; we have him as our leader because we represent the farmer's viewpoint in Canada. Food production is necessary in times of war. but it is no less vital in times of peace. Anyone who knows of the starving millions in the world to-day realizes that food is vital. We are receiving white cheese instead of butter; on Tuesdays and Fridays we cannot have meat; yet this is a great agricultural country. We begin to wonder what is wrong when we are told by former President Hoover and many others that millions will starve this coming winter. To my mind all other issues should be washed aside if we really live in an age when we believe in humanitarian principles. Should the unproven threat of inflation deter us in our efforts to meet this humanitarian need?
