speechtext:
If I knew as little about Massey-Harris as the hon. member does I would not be saying much about it. I followed the remarks of my hon. friend this afternoon very carefully. He followed the negative motion of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. He wants to cut down the wages that the labouring man receives rather than increase his earnings so that we can have a higher standard of living among working men.
Everyone knows that there is a food shortage in this dominion. Everyone knows that there are millions starving. It is common gossip in the barber shop, in the blacksmith shop, in garages, in the country store and on the street comer. What did Mr. Bevin, the British foreign minister, say the other day, and by the way he represents a government not quite as socialistic as my hon. friends to my left, but one that wants to assist labour? Mr. Bevin said: "Nazism, socialism and communism will be wiped out if we can feed the world." He went on to say that farm prices may be low for a year or two, but remember that food is so essential that we had better let farm prices rise and let wages rise so that labour can buy its products. That was Mr. Bevin. It was not the Tories speaking, but that is what we believe in too. Mr. Bevin was followed by the Right Hon. Mr. Amery who, speaking before the United States chamber of

I am not going to chide the Minister of Agriculture regarding agricultural implement prices because 'I understand he said that he heard it first over the radio. If he did, then he is in the same position as the rest of us, because nobody else heard it before. I am glad that he said in Melfort, Saskatchewan, if the price of farm implements was raised, farm prices should be raised. I am in agreement with him on that.
The Minister of Finance is worried about inflation. I recall that I suggested we should have compulsory savings twelve months before he adopted the policy. If the minister is so worried about inflation in connection with farm prices may I ask him why he suspended compulsory savings and1 threw into' the consumer market purchasing power of $250 million and added another $250 million in family bonuses, thereby adding half a billion dollars to purchasing power at a time when we were trying to keep the purchasing power down. This was all done at a time when we were paying over half a billion dollars in subsidies. Where is this money bo come from? Are we to sell our wheat at seventy-five cents less than what the world would1 pay for it? Are we to sell our bacon and beef for thirty per cent less than the United States would pay for it? Are we then going to ask the labour man, the white-collar worker, the industrialist who will employ the veterans, to pay this money? That is why I am opposed to the motion of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mrs. Strum). It is a negative motion. It says to labour, we will not give you any more; it encourages increases on farm implements. This party

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
stands for the removal of the ceiling on farm products so that the farm implement workers who make our products may get a reasonable standard of living. That is what we stand for. We believe in a reasonable standard of living for those who fought for victory. But where are these new fantastic economists who are pulling the golden rabbits out of the hat, going to find these billions of dollars?
When we have inflation, who will be the most responsible for it? The Minister of Finance has been most conscientious in trying to carry out this checkered shotgun policy of this government. But he knows very well that it will take ten times more revenue to carry this country under the policy of this government. When I came to this house first it took only one-tenth of what it does now to carry the expenditures of this country. The leading economists tell us we shall have to increase our national income, that we Shall have to increase it by 50 per cent if we are to maintain these new types of fantastic Liberal policies.
If we are going to increase our income by 50 per cent, and if it takes ten times as much more to run the country, why cannot the farmers at least get parity for their produce? I will not. support the subamendment, as 1 said, because it is a negative. I do not think the government will support it. But I believe that upon reconsideration-well, perhaps I should not say I believe it, because there are none so blind as those who will not see what these controls mean-so I will say that upon reconsideration they may not support our amendment.
In conclusion, I would ask what these controls mean. They mean that the consumers and the starving millions in Europe have the satisfaction of knowing about price ceilings in Canada, but they have no assurance that food products are being produced at a maximum.
Controls in wartime for the purpose of increasing production may be necessary. But the necessary powers granted to the executive in wartime are now being used to satisfy a lust for power in time of peace.
It may seem ridiculous, but I walked down a street in this fair city last Christmas, and I saw in the window an advertisement urging me to buy pyjamas for a dog. I walked into another store to buy a Christmas shirt for my son, but I could not get one. That is what happens under this type of controls. While national controls may be necessary in time of war. individual freedom is just as vital in peace. I know, as you know, Mr. Speaker, that if the farmers of Canada are prosperous the returned men will be employed and the 63260-1 Hi
farmers will be employed, and will be able to pay fair wages to the men who are employed, so that they can work and receive fair remuneration.
There has been misrepresentation by hon. members to your right, Mr. Speaker. . A few may cling to the methods of war time, to methods of dictatorship, but many will prefer the ways of peace.
Competition, reasonable pay for services, recompense for individual effort, choice of vocation-all these things are influenced by the. law of supply and demand. These are the main-springs of free enterprise. They are the corner-stones of democracy and of freedom. These are the bulwarks of democracy itself. That is our way of life. That is the freedom and the liberty described as victory.
The history of liberty is a history of the limitation of government control, not its increase.
I urge upon the government once more, in closing, that they give the farmers parity with other producers in Canada, so that we may feed the starving millions of Europe, and that other business may be assisted, and peace secured.
I urge upon the government to rescind some of these controls, and get rid of some of the controllers. After all, you know, many of them never milked a cow in their lives. We look forward to the day when these controls may be eliminated. This party stands for the elimination of price ceilings on agricultural production and wage controls, and in due course for the elimination of other price ceilings. I plead for the majority of the Canadian people, for the 600,000 or 700,000 farmers of Canada, and the 400,000 or 500,000 labourers, to help them to get proper returns, and in the end to obtain freedom and reasonable recompense for individual endeavour.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have heard the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) lodge perhaps
Price Ceiling-Farm Products

grain rate structure between eastern Canada and western Canada, and particularly as it detracts from Alberta's geographical advantage of using the province of British Columbia as a consuming market.
These matters are being discussed almost daily out there, and when the farmer reads that the railroads are likely to ask for permission to increase their freight rates, naturally he becomes extremely incensed because he knows that these applications for increased rates have been granted before and he concludes that they will be granted again.
We have a condenser in my constituency. Milk canned at that point and shipped to Vancouver pays a higher rate than that on the same quantity of milk canned in Ontario, say at Tillsonburg, and shipped to Vancouver. That is a most disturbing thing because, if we take into consideration the higher freight rate costs, the industry in Alberta cannot pay to the producer a comparable price to that paid in districts adjacent to Tillsonburg in Ontario.
We feel-I am speaking of the farmers- that we in that part of Canada are forced to absorb the shock from both east and west and on both exports and imports. I am pleased to know that the governments of the three prairie provinces have been able to get together with a view to prevail upon or assist, whichever you choose to call it, the Dominion of Canada in bringing about a more equitable freight rate structure in this country. I cannot see for a moment how you can grant justice to the farmers if that is not dpne.
Reference has been made here-and I constantly hear farmers referring to it-to marketing facilities. They insist upon adequate marketing facilities free from manipulation and monopoly control. They make particular reference to the live stock industry, and here the packers enter into the picture. A farmer handed me a clipping which he had evidently cut from a copy of the evidence given before the royal commission on price spreads in 1935. He showed me a statement which he said appeared between pages 59 and 60 of the price spreads report which was made by the president of Canada Packers Limited before that commission. It was this:
The total live stock is sold for the total sum, whatever it is; from that sum is deducted the packer's expense and the packer's profit and the farmer gets the balance.
Can one be surprised at our live stock producers being greatly agitated when they read a statement of that kind emanating from the then president of Canada Packers Limited? The evidence went on to point out that between 1929 and 1934, when the live stock industry, which is one branch of agriculture,

was taking such a terrible beating in western Canada, the profits [DOT] of the packing industry increased threefold.
The farmers say this to me repeatedly : We realize that the packers are in business to make a profit; we have no complaint against their making a legitimate profit because we ask the same opportunity for ourselves, and we realize too that the packing industry performs a useful function in the country. But they do not agree that a system should be permitted which enables those in the packing industry, which in effect is a monopoly, to thrive during a period when the primary producer does not receive a sufficient return to make it worth while for him to take his live stock to market. The profits of the packing industry increased between 1929 and 1934 by about 300 per cent. I should have mentioned that they wrote off repair charges and depreciation iii a scandalous fashion, and the price spreads commission reported accordingly, saying that if the repair charges and depreciation had been fair-I -will not say honest-the profits during that period would have been considerably greater. As the president of Canada Packers at that time said:
The total live stock is sold for the total sum, whatever it is; from that sum is deducted the packer's expense and the packer's profit and the farmer gets the balance.
Another matter to which we must pay h'eed if we- want stability in agriculture is the tariff. The farmers are discussing these matters much more frequently and much more intelligently than probably they did a few years ago, and this seems to be their general view with respect to tariffs. The farmers in my area believe that the tariff impoverishes the nation' by an amount much greater than the value of any non-material national purpose it may achieve, and I am personally in agreement with that view. They believe that tariffs should be reduced on commodities entering into the every-day cost of living. It is most essential that that be done so far as our western farmers are concerned. Moreover, they certainly believe that there should be a proper division of the national economic burden of tariffs, bearing in mind), of course, provincial populations. In the past, as shown by statistics presented during this debate, the farmers of the west have borne a tremendous load in connection with machine costs simply because of tariff barriers and embargoes designed', I say, to profit the industrialists of central Canada. They remember vividly out there, with respect to tariffs, the extent of the absolute burden during the depression. If I were to indicate four incidents with respect to tariffs which made it much more difficult

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
for the farmers during the depression years, I would refer to the enormous expansion of the number of items which were added from year to year to the tariff list, the increased import duties, the application of anti-dtanping legislation, and fixed values for duty purposes. Farmers certainly feel that the whole matter of tariffs will have to be carefully scrutinized, and that we must bring in a realistic policy if we are to have a flourishing, sound agriculture during these post-war years.
We cannot forget that in 1931 we in Alberta paid $8,211,148 in tariff subsidies to protected manufacturers. If I remember correctly, the Manitoba brief to the dominion-provincial conference estimated that the cost amounted to $110.38 per western farmer. Canadian farmers on that basis paid $32 million in the year 1931'because of tariff protection given to the manufacturers of central Canada. So that I think, when some people talk about the "poor relation in the west", the western farmer, they should bear in mind certain of the burdens which have been borne by those farmers because of protection granted to industries in central Canada.
As I stated early in my remarks, it is my firm belief that if we are to have a stable agriculture we must, as was indicated in his concluding remarks by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe, have parity prices established. I cannot see how we can avoid it. There is a great deal of argument as to exactly what "parity" means. There is a great deal of disagreement as to exactly how it should be established. I do not profess to be any expert, I do not presume to indicate how it could be established, but I say with certainty that we have in this country people capable of establishing it. In the second place, we must have during future years a long-range crop and live stock production programme in this country, not one just for this week or next month. I would say too, having in mind the various natural afflictions from which we suffer in the agricultural areas of the west, that we must establish a general crop insurance scheme. I would even go so far as to say that I personally feel it should be established on a noncontributory basis. We must arrange adequate low-cost credits for our western agriculturists. We must have equitable debt adjustment. The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras) indicated that farmers had paid approximately 50 per cent of their indebtedness. That is a tribute to the character of our farmers; it proves one thing, that they are willing to meet their obligations when they can, but it also proves that they still have on their shoulders 50 per cent of their burden. Moreover, I have known many farmers-hundreds
of farmers-who were completely out of debt but who, when prices went to rock bottom, soon found themselves hopelessly mired in debt again. With no control over the general price structure that may be the inevitable result. We must remove from our marketing facilities any manipulation which may exist and, certainly, monopoly control of the industry. Then, as I stated, we must also have adjustments in our freight rates structure and in our whole tariff set-up.
Let me emphasize also that one of the things which is bothering the farmer tremendously to-day is this question of taxation. He calls the tax collectors "predators"; some of them call them "pre-daters". I think all hon. members will agree that when a farmer, faced by conditions over which he has no control and which threaten to take from him everything he has accumulated over the years suddenly finds himself with an income which, though not large, is much better than he has ever had before, it is natural that upon being pounced on for taxes, even upon an income of only $1,200, and having part of it taken away, he chafes because he realizes that in all those years when he had next to nothing the dominion government was extremely reluctant and tardy in coming along and granting him the assistance which alone would make it possible for him to carry on. I think it is quite reasonable to suggest that the unmarried farmer should nqt be taxed on the first $1,200, or the married farmer on the first $2,000, of his income. I think also that, in bombarding us as the farmers have with requests for action in this regard, they are making a legitimate request. Let me assure the house that we over here took that stand long before we were bombarded with cards requesting that this course of action be taken.
I do not wish to take more of the time of the house, but let me emphasize, what I believe all hon. members know, that we cannot have a stable economy in Canada without having stability in our basic industry, namely agriculture.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate I want to deal particularly with the statements made in the motion of want of confidence moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken). First of all, however, may I say that I am sorry that the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) has now left the chamber. Though he was gibing at some members on this side for being new members and as not knowing what had occurred in the past in this house, I can speak as a member who has been here from 1930. I well remember sitting over there just about where the
Price Ceiling-Farm Products

leader of the opposition is sitting for the -moment, and during all the years from 1930 to 1935 I never heard the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) or the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe have much to say about the farmers. There was a silence over here regarding the farmer that could almost be felt. It went through my mind also that in the great campaign of 1930 his party slid in to office on butter. In 1930 they went through the province of Quebec and spoke about "fifty cents for butter"; and then I thought of the years 1930 to 1935 when butter was so cheap they were greasing axle wheels with it; cows were being sold for five to ten dollars, and eggs for seven to nine cents a dozen. I realize however, that to go back to those days and dwell on them now serves no really good purpose, but I mention it because I listened attentively to the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe, and his party is to be congratulated because about three times a year that kind of show is put on by the Progressive party.
I intended to deal particularly with the want of confidence motion of the leader of the opposition, and I am coming to that now. I believe that motion can be briefly stated in four sentences: A lessing production owing to the inequitable position of agriculture. Production down; dairy products, poultry and hogs. Canadian wheat should be the same price as in the United States, and the agricultural contribution, if so, amounts to about 3200 million. Finally, no justification in holding the price down.
To take the wheat statement first, everyone knows that wheat is the king-pin of our national economy, and I was surprised at what I term a loose statement made by the leader of the opposition, that he would take wheat, the king-pin of agriculture, remove the ceiling, and let it rise to the same price as in the United States. May I point out to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the house that the farmers of the United States are not any better off or as well off as the farmers of Canada. I just came across a press clipping which states that 2,000 farmers intend to leave what is called the good old United States where all these prices are received and come to northern Alberta and British Columbia, to God's country, the best country on earth. I am wondering if the leader of the opposition has considered what might happen and, in fact, what would happen if we were to follow the United States in regard to the price of wheat. I am surprised that when he spoke of the price of wheat he did not go farther and take in all other articles, for I think it can be said without fear of contradiction that if you lift the lid off wheat and all farm products 
you had better be prepared to lift the lid off everything. If that is the policy being enunciated by the leader of the opposition he should come out and tell this house-and the country that that is exactly what he means.
Let us see-ior a moment just what would happen in this country. If the price of wheat were raised to over 12 a bushel the first thing we would have to do would be to call in all the agreements we have with Great Britain and make a readjustment in regard to prices. We would have to say, "Well, when we settled these agreements with you and the prices were fixed, we agreed to give you wheat at the present set price. Now it has gone up to over 32"-and it would have to go to that price to equal the price in the United States-"we will have to raise prices and have new agreements." Just how that would work out no one can predict, but I am wondering if hon. members of the Progressive Conservative party have thought how the people of British Columbia would be affected if such a thing were to take place. As far as farming is concerned we in British Columbia go in principally for poultry, eggs and dairying, and we are a wheat purchasing province. We look to the prairies for our wheat, our barley and our oats, and the price there definitely affects the produce we have to sell. It is well known that were it not for the large subsidies paid at the present time by the government we could not carry on and make ends meet.
A few nights ago, when we were discussing the removal of the two-cent subsidy on milk, a thought entered my mind. I wondered if hon. members realized that the people of this country were paying the full price for milk anyway. If you look at the figures you will find that from 1939 to January of this year some $23,888,666 has been paid by the people of Canada in that two-cent subsidy on milk. So that when we speak of the price of milk being increased, let us not overlook the fact that the people have been paying this two cents right along. But it is well known that the nicest way to tax people is not to let them know they are being taxed at all, as we collect the sales tax and so on, by taking it from them indirectly. But when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) brings down his budget and we come to discuss the income tax no doubt we shall hear a cry for increased subsidies and lower taxation. Just how those will be reconciled I do not know, and I doubt if even the minister will be able to reconcile them. But what about the other commodities if our wheat prices follow those of the United States? Wheat is but one thing. Lift that lid and the ceiling is off as regards everything else.

Price Ceiling-Farm Products.

I do not think I need waste a great deal of time saying why. In the first place, wheat is the king-pin, and if you removed the ceiling on wheat every other commodity would demand the same treatment. Do you think for a moment that labour and the manufacturers would remain quiet if you permitted the price ceiling to go where it liked? But I am going to leave this thought with hon. gentlemen opposite, and with the leader of the opposition. Are we going now to adopt the policy that in times like the present, when prices a little better than those guaranteed may be obtained, shall allow the prairie farmers to be free agents and go into the world markets to obtain those prices; and then when wheat drops to away below a dollar have them turn around and say it is up to the state to assist or protect them?
Personally I do not think you can have it both way. If the state is to take an interest in the farmer when the price is low, in my opinion the state should take an interest when the price is likely to go out of sight. To my mind, the policy suggested by the Progressive Conservative party is extremely short-sighted, and I shall give my reasons for making that statement.

speechtext:
At least. That will do for the present, and that answers my hon. friend's question. For the next five years at least the price will never go below that figure. The farmer is assured of SI.55 at the present time, because he gets SI.25, less the freight to Vancouver or Fort William, and then he participates in sales of wheat abroad at whatever price is obtained. That is the picture as I get it from the Department of Agriculture, and generally speaking, I think that
is a correct statement. Surely the guarantee to the farmer is worth something. Surely it is of some advantage to be guaranteed a definite minimum return. In a moment or two I am going to dispute, and try to prove my point with figures, that price has not been the principal reason if there has been any drop in agriculture. I am going to take the statements made by the leader of the opposition, and I am going to give the authority for any figures I quote. I believe that when figures are quoted in this house the source of the figures should be definitely stated, so that one hon. member is not quoting from one source and another from some other source. I have gone to the bureau of statistics for the figures I am going to quote, and I am sure no one will accuse the bureau of statistics of being a partisan body. I have kept away from the Department of Agriculture and any other department. To-night I am sticking to the figures of the bureau of statistics.
Before I deal with that, may I say that it is a well-known fact that farmers are not satisfied. I know of no group of individuals in this country who are satisfied. Even members of parliament are not satisfied. I have met members of parliament who have received an increase of $2,000 and some of them are not satisfied. I know that some have attended the sittings fewer times since they received the increase than formerly. I say that as one who has been present at every sitting. No group in Canada is satisfied. No one seems to be satisfied. And so the farmers are not the only class of people who are not satisfied.
The leader of the opposition said that the production of dairy products is down. He mentioned poultry and hogs. From the figures I received from the bureau I find that the statement made by the leader of the opposition is not correct in so far as dairy products and poultry are concerned. I hold in my hand the years and the millions of pounds of production of meat in Canada as given by the dominion bureau of statistics. I find that more beef has been produced up to 1945, which is the highest year since 1935. More veal was produced. There was more mutton and lamb produced in 1945. There was a greater production of turkey and chicken in 1945 than in 1943' and 1944, or the average between 1935 and 1939. Therefore the statement made by the leader of the opposition should be corrected. I am endeavouring to correct it to-night and put on the record the exact figures given to me rather than just make a general statement. It is all very well to make a general statement and say that production is down. I am placing these figures on Hansard
Price Ceiling-Farm. Products

to-night, so that any hon. member may check them later and refute them later if he cares to do so.
If one goes over the list of products of agriculture he will find that, on the average, the production is not down from 1935 to 1945 except in some few instances. Here again the leader of the opposition has not mentioned the effect the weather has, and it is a fact that the weather influences our crops.
The leader of the opposition dealt particularly with wheat. I looked over the figures for wheat, oats, barley, hay and clover, and I found that in 1940 there were 54-1 million acres in all sown; in 1945 there were 55-4 million acres sown; in other words, there were T3 million acres more. Regarding wheat, with almost the same acreage as in 1945, the production of wheat was 129-6 million bushels greater in 1944. The same thing applies to barley. With the same acreage in barley the crop in 1944 -was 36-9 million bushels greater than in 1945. Oats with the same acreage produced 118 million bushels more in 1944 than in 1945. Hay and clover were a little less. In fact, in 1941, with two million acres less, on the average the wheat crop in that year was greater by nine million bushels. Why? Because of weather conditions. But the leader of the opposition tried to leave the impression and I believe he partly succeeded in certain quarters, that the production of agriculture was the result of the policies of this government and the prices that are being paid. I claim that that is somewhat of an indictment of the farmers, because with nearly 400,000 fewer people on the farm they have, since 1939, been producing more year after year. The production in 1945 shows an increase in most instances. It certainly shows an increase in dairy products and in poultry. It is true that hogs dropped down a little. Milk production is about the same level in 1945 as in 1944.
There is one element that enters into the fact that our people are not keen to go on the land, which was not mentioned by the leader of the opposition, namely, the attitude of labour to-day. With fewer men on the farm, with more machinery, farmers are producing generally more than they did in 1939 or 1940. When young men read of the proposals of certain labour organizations, some of which are asking for a six-day week, $25 a week minimum pay, time and a half for overtime after thirty-six hours, double time for Sundays and statutory holidays, and the payment of at least $25 per week for the full period of unemployment, is it any wonder that many men cannot be induced to stay on or go back to the farm? I do not know whether Your
Honour has farmed, but farming is one of the occupations where you just cannot put it over old mother nature. You have to work on the farm. You get up early in the morning and you work long hours, or you do not stay long on the farm. With the trends that are taking place and the way things are going, is -it any wonder that many young men are thinking as they are and drifting into the cities by the thousands?	.
If the leader of the opposition had been covering the whole gamut of our life it is a wonder he did not suggest the following for the farmers: For cleaning the stables and hauling the manure the farmer should have at least as much as the garbage collector; for eighty per cent of the time that he is working as a scientific agriculturist he should have an hourly rate of pay equal to that of the skilled mechanic; for working as a business manager he should be paid as much as a business man with similar investments; for the money he has invested he should have returns comparable with the earnings on money invested at comparable risks. He should have all this income but he has never had half of it. Farming, of course, cannot be put on a dollar-and-cents basis, because farming is not altogether a business; it is a means of living, a mode of life, and those of us who live on the farm do so because we love that kind of life or occupation.
I come back again to what the leader of the opposition dealt with in his endeavour to leave the impression that the drop in agricultural production was due to the policy of this government. I say that it was an irresponsible statement made by a responsible public man, because I believe it is contrary to the facts, as can be seen if one analyses all the facts carefully.
Speaking about labour conditions, I say it is one of the greatest indictments of our country that we have to keep here something like seventeen thousand German prisoners of war to work in pulp camps and sugar beet districts. If they stay here much longer I would be surprised if some champions on their behalf will not later rise and say these men saved agriculture in the years 1945 and 1946. I repeat, it seems almost an indictment of our people that these men are remaining. Personally I should have like to see them taken out of this country just as soon after the defeat of Germany as possible, because these men have been bred in nazism and should not be left any longer in Canada.
I heard the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) speak about being friendly to labour. I am sorry he is not in his place

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
at the moment because I was going to deal particularly with German labour in so far as he was concerned. If I never got a man to work for me I certainly would never take a nazi. I submit that these men should have been sent back long ago. But if you are going to lift the ceiling on wheat and provide the same price as they receive in the United States, then let us go all the way. If that is what the leader of the opposition wants, why does he not say so? It is all very well for him to advocate a wheat policy, but if inflation overtakes us who will be held responsible by the Canadian people? This government will be held responsible, and that is where the difference lies. This government is responsible for the welfare of the people of this country. But when one is in opposition these statements can be made, because if anything disastrous happened-and I claim it would happen if the ceilings were taken off-the entire blame would then rest with the present government. What would happen in British Columbia and elsewhere in Canada if there were no ceiling price on lumber? I know some people in British Columbia who are so eager to get lumber that they would gladly pay $100 for a thousand feet of it. We are thankful for the fact that there is a ceiling price on it. But that is only but one example.
We produce enough lumber for our own people, but there are other factors which enter into the sale and disposal of Canadian lumber. There is the matter of shipping our lumber to Great Britain and keeping our trade both with Britain and the United States open, and let us not forget that the United States supply us with 50 per cent of our coal. One might ask why we do not produce all the coal here, and why we have to depend upon the United States.
In the past year more lumber was produced in Canada than in any other year in our history. But, as everyone knows, we are supplying Great Britain and a certain percentage is going to the United States. Those are markets which must be maintained. The lumber manufacturers have said thus far, without contradiction, that if all the lumber in this country were sold in Canada the price would jump from $15 to $25 a thousand immediately, due to labour costs and the price of logs which they purchased in the open market. That statement has never been refuted.
Let us again look at prices in the United States. All our fishermen who catch fish in Canadian waters, on both the Atlantic and the Pacific, would have to get the same price as they get in the United States. Workers would have to receive the same pay. Where would it all end? The whole thing comes down to
this that the people in the United States are not in as good position as we are in Canada, where price ceilings have been kept down by the present government.
My chief reason for rising this evening was to deal with the statements made by the leader of the opposition. My analysis and my reading of the figures presented by the bureau of statistics certainly do not bear out what he said. The only conclusion one can draw from his statement is that the price of wheat in this country should follow the United States price. He and his party evidently are in favour of lifting the lid off price ceilings. I say to the people of this country, God help us if that happens.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was glad to hear the hon. member for Dufferin-S'imcoe (Mr. Rowe) make clear to the house the policy of the Progressive Conservative party. The party for which he was speaking this evening wants controls lifted from everything. I think reasonable people in Canada everywhere know that this would mean inflation. And when the spiral of inflation comes, the workers, farmers, small business people and professional people are caught in that spiral and suffer tremendously.
It has been suggested by many hon. members that the workers and farmers do not see eye-to-eye on the policy of price increases. May I point out that recently in Saskatchewan the United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan section, the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, the Canadian Congress of Labour and the Saskatchewan Teachers' Federation set up the Saskatchewan occupational group council and issued a joint statement respecting their policy-on ceiling prices.
First of all, they pointed out that as a solution of the spiralling of prices we request the reestablishment of price ceilings as legally in force in August, 1944. Further they said:
We agree with the principles of parity prices, and we suggest it be placed upon the basis of $1.55 per bushel for wheat, with a royal commission appointed to set all items and wages in comparison thereto.
That organization representing farmers, labourers and professional people went on record as supporting parity prices, and saying that $1.55 a bushel for wheat Was something close to parity price. They also asked that the government provide equal representation of all occupational groups, on the wartime prices and trade board, or on any other price control board. This agrees with the policy of the C.C.F. as enunciated many times, in that any board having to do with the making of policy affecting the people of Canada in an economic
Price Ceiling-Farm Products

way should have on it representatives of the farmers, the industrial workers, small business and the professional people in Canada.
The council further stated that if any logical reason were given by the government why the requests for a return to the price ceilings of 1944, with certain exceptions, were not followed, then they supported the stand of the United Farmers for a 20 per cent increase in the prices of grain. They, too, were supporting a policy of parity prices, because they said that if the cost of things the farmer has to buy goes up then prices of commodities the farmer has to sell should also go up.
The leader of the Progressive Conservative party (Mr. Bracken), speaking on his amendment, made certain that he did not criticize the government in any respect for having allowed the 12% per cent increase in the price of farm implements. He did not say that the implement companies were not deserving of it. One can see, if he reads the speeches of members of the Progressive Conservative party, that they are supporting big business from one end of Canada to the other-and I shall be the first to admit that they are doing a fine job of it.
Much has been said in the debate about the reduction in the selling costs of farm implements. It is true that there has been a considerable reduction. I do not think the precise nature of that reduction in selling costs has been pointed out to the house. When we understand how the reduction has taken place we shall see that it is permanent, and1 that in some respects it has ifot been brought about in the most admirable way.
Ten years ago, if a man in a small town were in the implement business, he was an implement agent. He had little to invest by way of capital. That man was simply the contact man for the implement companies. He talked to farmer customers and drew up a slate of prospects for various implements. He sent that slate of prospects to the implement companies, and they in turn sent a salesman to the town. The agent would get into the salesman's car and they would go out to the farmer's home. Then, if a sale took place, and payment were to be made on time basis, the company would take the responsibility of making collections. The agent would receive his commission, and he had nothing to lose as long as the sale went through.
Then, too, the companies used to stock repairs for implement agents. Every once in a while the auditor would come around and check the stock of repair parts, and the agent would be asked to pay for the repair parts

he had sold. The point is that the implement agents were not forced to take any credit risks and were not asked to put a great deal of their money into the business.

Perhaps twenty per cent of those people are now dealers and they are in a much different position from what they were in when they were agents. A dealer must put in a complete machine repair and service shop. He must hire mechanics and supply tools. He must carry his own stock of repair parts. He must buy the machines from the company and sell them to the farmers.' If we get back to time sales in the future, should any loss occur the implement dealer will absorb it and the implement company will lose nothing because, as soon as a machine leaves their hands, it is completely paid for. I want to point out the growing monopolization in the implement distribution field. The small business man no longer has a chance of making a living; instead he is asked to put thousands of dollars of his own money into a very risky business. When the squeeze, comes he is the one who will be squeezed^ out. In presenting his statement to the house after the increase had taken place, the minister said as reported at page 853 of Hansard:
In their submissions the companies disclosed increased costs since the basic period of 1941 averaging, roughly, materials and components twenty per cent, labour twenty-eight and a half per cent, and general overhead twenty-three per cent.
I think it would have been fairer to the people of Canada generally and to hon. members if we had been given an opportunity to hear the submissions made by the implement companies, to conduct a thorough investigation into those submissions and then attempt to find out if increases were necessary and, if so, how much they should be. I wonder what part of that increase was due to the increase of $5 a ton in the price of steel allowed some time previously. When steel was increased $5 a ton it meant that in each process in which steel was used there was a pyramiding of the S5 a ton increase. If any of the increase in the cost of materials was

due to the increase in the price of steel, then this government is responsible for the increased cost of materials.
We were told by the implement companies that the cost of labour has increased 28J per cent. On looking at the report of the parliamentary committee which sat in 1937 to consider farm implement prices, I find that of the labour costs of producing a machine, 51 per cent was indirect labour. Of that indirect labour, one-quarter was for the payment of foremen and foremen's assistants and one-third was for the wages of factory executives and clerical workers. I should like to know if any large part of that 28J per cent increase in the cost of labour is due to large increases in the wages paid to foremen and factory executives.

I shall deal with him in a minute. The minister went on to state, as reported at page 852 of Hansard:
I should add that the analysis of costs conducted by the prices board indicated that a price increase' of upwards of 30 per cent above 1941 levels would have been required to regain 1941 profit percentage margins for the farm implement industry. Consequently, the price advance of only 12| per cent means, admittedly, a serious profit squeeze upon the industry.
I am going ahead to prove that that statement is not in accordance with the evidence as we have it in this house, nor is it in accordance with the statistics to which we have access. The increase of 30 per cent refers to factory costs, and the parliamentary assistant stated that. What we want to know is what the 12i per cent increase in the retail price means when it is applied to the factory cost. I have before me the proceedings of the special committee on farm implement prices, and on page 138 is a table setting out the total costs and sales realizations of typical implements manufactured in Canada. This table gives the cost of the various items going into a ,machine. The retail price is taken as 100, and over a long period of years the cost of materials is shown to be 27-01 per cent of the retail price. We are told that the material cost increased 20 per cent. If that is so, then a 5-4 per cent increase in the retail price would take care of the increase in the material cost.
It is stated in this table that the labour cost is equal to 8-64 per cent of the retail selling price. We were told by the Minister of Finance that the labour cost had increased 284 per cent. In order completely to cover the increased cost of labour the retail selling price needed to be increased only 2-46 per cent. We should not be told any more that prices are going up because labour is getting more. I have shown by these statistics that the claimed increase in labour costs amounts to only 2-46 per cent of the retail selling price. We are told by the implement companies that the burden cost increased 23 per cent. The parliamentary committee found that the burden cost was 13-89 per cent of the retail price. That cost has gone up 23 per cent, so that an increase of 3-19 per cent in the retail cost of farm machines would have fully compensated the companies for the increased burden which they claim took place. Instead, the government gave the implement companies a 124 per cent increase on all implements. The total increase in the retail selling price that would have been necessary to cover all the increased material costs, labour costs and burden costs claimed by the companies is 11-05 per cent. So that the claim by the government that they drove a hard bargain cannot be substantiated by the facts. After they came out of the conference with the implement companies, they gave the companies 11 per cent more in a retail price increase than would have covered all the increases in all the costs which the companies claimed had taken place.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know I am speaking for a great majority of the people in the constituency I represent when I say that it would be disastrous to have price ceilings removed at the present time. It might be of benefit to the few, but generally, I feel, it would be responsible for making the rich richer and the poor poorer.
I personally am much more interested in having fair prices permanently placed on products of the farms and the sea than I am in having ceiling prices removed. There is an old saying that a burned child dreads the fire. I believe it would apply in this case, because many of us should remember that period during the first great war and the years following when millionaires were made overnight and less fortunate people with small incomes were unable to have more than the bare necessities of life.
As to price ceilings discouraging the production of needed food, I feel this has to a great extent been responsible for increasing production, because the primary producer
Price Ceiling-Farm Products

could plan with some guarantee of security, knowing he would not be obliged to sell his product below the cost of production.
This security would have been greatly appreciated in the constituency I represent prior to the war and, I am sure, will be in future years if sustained by this government. Production will never fall on account of price ceilings. The same cooperation as was exemplified during the war, under difficulties relative to the shortage of man-power, will, I am sure, continue and be further increased if these people are given a chance to produce. With world conditions as we find them to-day, these men that I speak of will not let us down. Production may fall during this year. If it does, it w'ill not be owing to any lack of the energy or will to produce, but to matters beyond the control of the producer.
It is true that a small percentage of the farmers in Charlotte depend on farming alone for their livelihood. The great proportion depend to a great extent on the products of the forests, the pulpwood, lumber, firewood and boxwood which they usually cut in the winter time. Prices paid for these commodities during the war have been encouraging. If one compares prices being paid1 for these commodities to-day with those paid in 1940 he will find that they compare favourably with price increases in labour or manufactured products.	(
The argument in favour of this movement would seem to be relative to the agricultural industry. I realize the important part this industry plays in the general welfare of this country, and I feel it warrants great consideration, because it would affect every province and ,a great proportion of bur population. Might I remark, this industry is well represented in this house, not only by an able minister; but, from my obesrvations since I have been here, I would say that three-fourths of the members of this house represent agricultural communities, and I would also say that three-fourths of the time of this house 'have been taken up in discussing matters pertaining to agriculture. ,
It would appear that too few people realize that there are other primary producers in Canada than farmers, and that their problems might be quite as important to them as to the problem now under discussion is to the farmers. I wish to make my position clear; I do not want to give the impression in any way that 1 consider the farming industry unimportant. It is one of our greatest industries, and certainly I regard it as such. In the past, prices of farm products have fluctuated greatly, but I should like to point

out certain advantages which this industry has always had as compared with the products of the sea. The fisherman has an extremely perishable products, which must be sold immediately it is taken from the sea. It cannot be held indefinitely awaiting better market conditions. Therefore the producer is always at the mercy of the canner and exporter and must accept whatever they have to offer. That is why I am very much interested in floor prices. I feel that it would be a selfish attitude for any primary producer to take to ask for floor prices without also having ceiling prices. From past experience- and this is my own experience-I would say that the fishermen of the constituency I represent certainly would support floor prices.
During the war years the price of sardines was set by international agreement between canners in Canada and the state of Maine. This was necessary since a great part of the sardines caught in Charlotte county are exported to Maine in the fresh state. I feel that I am speaking for every sardine fisherman in Charlotte when I say that nothing would please them more or give them a greater feeling of security than to know definitely that the prices now set would be continued during the next five years or longer; and fishermen in other branches of the industry would be of the same. opinion. Since prices during the past five years have been fair, their prosperity has been based solely upon their ability to produce.
The increase in the prices of farm implements has been debated and criticized by a great many hon. members. In most instances it was urged that the farmer should have an increase in the prices paid for his products or that the government should absorb the increase by way of subsidies. No doubt there would be some justification for this argument, and under certain conditions I feel that from time to time adjustments will be necessary. But might I point out that since the ceiling price on sardines was established materials used in the construction of sardine weirs-and I want hon. members to listen very carefully- have increased in price by 300 per cent. Unlike farm machinery, the greater part o.f this material has to be replaced each year, costing each sardine fisherman hundreds and, in some instances thousands of dollars annually.

In conclusion, I should like to quote from an article which appeared in the Montreal Daily Star of May 11, 1946. The element of party politics seems consistently in evidence. In the very few minutes that remain, I should like to make a few remarks on an aspect of price control. I do so especially because I wish to refer to some remarks made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) in this house in December last. I hope I realize the difficulties that face those who are dealing with price controls. I do not speak at all lightly of this subject. There are certain necessities, particularly things like rent, where I think price control has been justified and, so far as my opinion goes, is still justified. But it seems to me that what we entirely lack is any indication of principle, and, indeed, any indication of practice to give one an idea as to the directions in which the mind of the government is moving. I should like to read briefly some remarks made by the Minister of Finance on December 18 last, and then refer to him an instance which has come to my own attention quite recently. I do this in the hope that quite possibly it may be of some interest to him; and it might even lead to certain reconsiderations of what was done, not so much in this case, because it has been taken care of in another way, but a reconsideration of the principle which guided the department in this case. The remarks of the minister that I wish to read are based upon a question that I asked him in December last. I said, granted we need controls on necessaries, does that apply to luxuries and does that apply in particular to a thing like jewellery? Here is what the minister said, as reported at page 3738 of Hansard:
I have discussed the" matter with the officials and I have put the question to them: Why can you not take the price ceiling off jewellery and a long list of other things? We have gone into that question very fully, and it is extraordinarily difficult to do it unless you see the end of price control in sight, because you cannot pick out any class of things that do not enter in some form into the cost of other things. As I say, I have no time to enter into it in detail, but it is most difficult. The policy now is an over-all price ceiling, with an increasing tendency toward increases on certain articles.
Having referred to that, I wish to bring to the attention of the minister and of the house a small incident that came to my attention a week or two ago. I was communicated with by two friends of mine who were blacksmiths in Huntsville. They told me that they had applied for an increase in their schedule, and had been turned down. I got in touch with wartime prices and trade board and explained the difficulty to them. They were sympathetic, and I am bound to say that I used the expression that I thought controls on small things like this are fantastic. I could not really believe they entered importantly into the

question of inflation. I thought the official to whom I talked was sympathetic to what I said. In fact, what he said to me was this; he asked me to let the matter stand for a week. From the way he talked I got the impression-and I think I was entitled to get it-that he hoped within a week the ceiling might be taken off. I called him up a week later, and he said to me that it had not been possible to take the ceiling off but that they were dealing with the matter in another way by giving it an increase of rate. They did give the increase of rate, and I think the particular problem of my friends is dealt with for the moment.
The reason I raise this point-and I am glad the minister is in the house to-night- is that I submit to him and to this house that surely we are getting doctrinaire views on patterns-I think that was the word the minister used; that it all fits into a pattern. Surely that does take us on extraordinary lengths into the matter of doctrinaire views. Here is a man shoeing horses in Huntsville. Incidentally, I believe the price that he asked was perfectly agreeable to the people who were asked to pay it. His present schedule was clamped down at a time when prices had been going on unchanged for many years. This price is clamped down on him, and his costs have gone up in the interval. He and his friends were perfectly agreeable to reaching an agreement among themselves, but they could not do that because of the pattern. That is my story. It is a simple thing, but I submit to the minister that at the present time what people are groping for is something in the way of a principle. It is hard for me to believe that any principle of orderly and .common-sense release of controls is in practice when a small thing of that kind can take place and be given effect to. I was saying to the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) this evening that one of the few Latin tags I could still remember from my time as a law student was, de minimis non curat lex which means, "the law does not concern itself with little things". I suggest that should also apply to the wartime prices and trade board.
Finally, I would say that if I am right in my attitude toward this particular case, and if I am right in assuming, as I did assume, that it is symptomatic of a great many others, then it seems to me that there is a great deal of room for ordinary common sense to be introduced into the subject of controls, difficult as I admit it to be.

speechtext: I move that the house do now adjourn. With regard to to-morrow, this debate will be continued and, I devoutly hope, will be concluded. If it is, we should like to call at least three departments in committee of supply. The departments would be labour, post office' and veterans affairs, and. also having priority I should say over calling these departments even would be the matter of interim supply. We have run out of money and we need some more. I have to get interim supply to-morrow some way or another, or the carrying on of the public business will be seriously prejudiced.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: If I may comment on the minister's remarks I should like to say that there will be no objection from this party to putting more departments into supply, and we shall be glad to facilitate the voting of interim supply. I may say that the minister spoke to me about this a day ago. I complained, and I think with justice, that this particular motion had been held up for three weeks. I take some responsibility for suggesting to the minister that it ought to be dealt with, I said it was not fair to this section of the house to have the motion standing day after day and not dealt with. The minister has been good enough to bring on the debate. There will be no disposition on the part of this party to extend the debate at all, but I feel that it should be dealt with. Once it has been disposed of, we shall facilitate in every way the granting of interim supply. There may be some questions on detail. The minister has already had two months' interim supply and he now wants two months more. In addition to that, he wants something extra for some departments which require more funds in the earlier part of the year than in the latter part of the year. I should think that the house would be disposed to meet any reasonable request that the minister makes with respect to the granting of interim supply.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I wish to thank the leader of the opposition for his offer of cooperation in the matter of interim supply.
With regard to the holding up of this debate, I felt that we were proceeding as fast as we could, with one exception, and that was the absence of myself from Ottawa for two days. That was unavoidable, and it brought about the chief delay in proceeding with the debate, I believe those days were Monday and Tuesday of last week.
Immediately upon my return we proceeded with the debate. However, be that as it may, we hope to conclude this debate to-morrow
and get into supply. If we should finish interim supply, and get those three departments in, we' shall be free to take up any other bills or resolutions on the order paper. But I doubt whether there will be much time for that, it being Wednesday.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: It is not clear to me why there should be three departments brought in.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Only five departments are in at the present time, and to facilitate the work of the house we thought we should have three more. There are twenty or more departments to come, and that will give ample opportunity for motions on going into supply to make known grievances. What I am suggesting is, I feel sure, in accordance with the practice of former years.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 11.05 p.m.
Wednesday, May 22, 1946.
